text: Golda Meir (originally Meyerson; née Mabovitch; born 3 May 1898 – died 8 December 1978) was the prime minister of Israel from 1969 to 1974 and the country's first and only female head of government. Born into a Jewish family in downtown Kiev (now Kyiv), present-day Ukraine, then part of the Russian Empire, she was the daughter of Blume Neiditch and Moshe Yitzhak Mabovitch, a carpenter. Meir had two sisters, Sheyna (born 1889) and Tzipke (later Clara; born 1902), and five siblings who died in infancy. Her earliest memories included her father boarding up the front door in response to rumors of a pogrom. She was named after her grandmother Golde. In 1903, Moshe left Russia for New York City, and after his absence, the family moved to Pinsk, present-day Belarus. In 1905, he moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where he found work in the railroad yard workshops and saved enough money to bring his family to the United States. Meir, along with her parents and sister, arrived in Quebec and traveled to Milwaukee by train. Blume ran a grocery store on Milwaukee’s north side, and by age eight, Meir often managed the store. She attended the Fourth Street Grade School (now the Golda Meir School) from 1906 to 1912 and, as a leader, organized the American Young Sisters Society in 1908 to fund her classmates’ textbooks. She graduated as valedictorian despite frequent tardiness due to work. In 1912, she began studying at North Division High School and worked part-time at Schuster’s department store and the Milwaukee Public Library. Her parents wanted her to marry and leave school, but she declined. In 1914, after a disagreement with her sister, she left North High School, moved out, and found work. After reconciling with her parents, she returned to Milwaukee and resumed studies, graduating in 1915. She became an active member of Young Poale Zion, which later became Habonim, embracing Socialist Zionism. In 1916, she attended the Milwaukee State Normal School (now University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee), and in 1917, she took a position at a Yiddish-speaking Folks Schule, further embracing Labor Zionism. On 9 July 1917, she became a naturalized U.S. citizen by descent, as her father had naturalized. On 24 December 1917, she married Morris Meyerson, with the condition that they settle in Palestine. Her plans to immigrate immediately were disrupted when transatlantic passenger services were canceled due to the U.S. entering World War I, so she focused on Poale Zion activities. After the war ended in 1921, the couple moved to Mandatory Palestine with Meir’s sister Sheyna, Sheyna’s daughter, and her childhood friend Regina, arriving via the SS Pocahontas from New York to Naples and then by train to Tel Aviv. Meir’s parents followed in 1926. The family was accepted into kibbutz Merhavia in the Jezreel Valley after an initial rejection; her duties included picking almonds, planting trees, working in chicken coops, and running the kitchen. Recognizing her leadership, the kibbutz elected her as its representative to the Histadrut. In 1924, the couple left Merhavia and lived briefly in Tel Aviv before settling in Jerusalem, where they had two children: Menachem (1924) and Sarah (1926). Meir returned to Merhavia in 1925. In 1928, she was elected secretary of Moetzet HaPoalot (Working Women's Council), and from 1932 to 1934, she served in the United States as an emissary to obtain medical treatment for her daughter’s kidney illness. In 1934, upon returning from the U.S., she joined the Executive Committee of the Histadrut and became head of its Political Department, a key training role for her future leadership. In July 1938, she served as the Jewish observer at the Évian Conference, where delegates from 32 countries expressed sorrow over Jewish refugees but refused to admit them; the only exception was the Dominican Republic, which pledged 100,000 refugees. Meir expressed disappointment and stated, "There is only one thing I hope to see before I die and that is that my people should not need expressions of sympathy anymore." During World War II, she held several key roles in the Jewish Agency, the Zionist Organization’s arm in British Palestine. In June 1946, after the British arrested Moshe Sharett and other Yishuv leaders in Operation Agatha, Meir became acting head of the Political Department, becoming the principal negotiator between the Jewish community and the British. After Sharett left for the U.S. to attend UN Partition Plan talks, Meir led the department until Israel’s establishment in 1948. In 1947, she traveled to Cyprus to meet Jewish detainees in internment camps and successfully persuaded them to prioritize families with children for entry into Palestine. On 17 November 1947, she met King Abdullah I of Jordan, who was seen as the only Arab leader willing to ally with a future Israeli state; the meeting confirmed his unwillingness to invade and his willingness to cooperate. Throughout the war, Meir played a minor role, feeling pushed aside, but she was critical in fundraising. In January 1948, the Jewish Agency needed funds for the war and the new state; the treasurer believed they could raise only $7 to $8 million from the American Jewish community, but Meir raised over $30 million, largely due to an emotional speech delivered in Chicago on 22 January. She toured dozens of U.S. cities and returned to Israel on 18 March. The funds were vital to the war effort, as the Arab Higher Committee’s annual budget was around $2.25 million, similar to Haganah’s pre-war budget. Ben-Gurion later called her the "Jewish woman who got the money which made the state possible." However, upon returning, she was excluded from the 13-member cabinet of the provisional government and included in the 37-member People's Council, a decision Ben-Gurion protested as "inconceivable" and "a moral and political necessity." On 13 April, she was hospitalized in Tel Aviv due to a suspected heart attack; Ben-Gurion and political leaders urged her to recover and take on the role of "mother of this city," believing her words would inspire 100,000 residents. Instead, on 6 May, she visited Haifa after its occupation by Haganah and described the mass expulsion and flight of Arabs as "dreadful," likening it to the fate of Jews in Nazi-occupied Europe. She returned to Tel Aviv and eventually to Jerusalem two weeks before the end of the mandate. On 11 May, she met Abdullah I again, after being denied a meeting at Naharayim due to safety concerns and being forced to travel to Amman in secret as an Arab woman. At the meeting, Abdullah claimed he had made a promise when alone but now was "one of five" and could not fulfill it alone. He proposed integrating Jordan into Palestine with Jewish representation in the Jordanian parliament, but Meir refused. The meeting ended without agreement, and Abdullah stated he would be forced to invade due to Arab League pressure. Meir expressed openness to meeting again after Israel won the war. On 14 May 1948, Meir became one of 24 signatories (including two women) of the Israeli Declaration of Independence, recalling that she cried upon signing, saying she could not imagine real people doing such a thing. A day after independence, the second phase of the war began, and Meir lost her administrative role as the Political Department became the provisional Ministry of Foreign Affairs, with Dov Yosef taking over in Jerusalem. On 18 May, she launched a second fundraising tour, raising around $50 million, bringing her total fundraising to about $90 million—roughly one-third of the war’s $275 million cost. During preparations, she was issued the first Israeli passport. Over ten weeks, Israel faced significant war changes. On 25 June, while still in the U.S., she was appointed by Sharett as minister plenipotentiary to the Soviet Union, which had recently recognized Israel. Meir was displeased, as she spoke no Russian and feared loneliness in Moscow, stating, "At last we have a state. I want to be there. I don't want to go thousands of miles away. Why do I always have to go away?" Her return was delayed by a car crash that injured her leg and fractured a bone; Soviet officials refused to believe she was in the hospital and insisted on her return, so she ignored medical advice and returned on 29 July. She served as minister plenipotentiary from 2 September 1948 to 10 March 1949. She was impatient with diplomatic niceties and interpreters, did not drink or ballroom dance, and had little interest in gossip or fashion. When asked by a Russian ambassador how she traveled to Moscow, she replied, "tell His Excellency the Ambassador that we arrived riding on donkeys." This role was significant and difficult, as good Soviet relations affected Israel’s access to arms from Eastern Europe. Stalin and Molotov viewed the relationship as a tool for advancing Soviet influence in the Middle East. Soviet policies against religious and nationalist movements, including closing Jewish religious institutions and banning Hebrew language study and emigration to Israel, complicated relations. Just 20 days after her appointment, antisemitic crackdowns began in response to an article by Ilya Ehrenburg. Meir and her team responded by visiting Russian Jewish businesses, synagogues, and cultural events. On 3 October, during Rosh Hashanah at the Moscow Choral Synagogue, she was mobbed by thousands of Russian Jews chanting "Nasha Golda" ("Our Golda"), an experience she described as overwhelming and heart-stopping. Soviet–Israeli relations were complicated by Soviet policies targeting religious institutions and nationalist movements, including the shutdown of Jewish religious institutions, the ban on Hebrew language study, and the prohibition of promoting emigration to Israel. Just 20 days after her term began, antisemitic crackdowns started in response to an article by Soviet Jewish writer Ilya Ehrenburg. Meir and other Israeli representatives responded by visiting Russian Jewish businesses, synagogues, and cultural events. On 3 October, during Rosh Hashanah at the Moscow Choral Synagogue, she was mobbed by thousands of Russian Jews chanting "Nasha Golda," meaning "Our Golda," an event she described as overwhelming and emotionally powerful, with her heart slowing from the intensity of the love. This moment was commemorated by the Israeli 10,000-shekel banknote issued in November 1984, which featured her portrait on one side and the image of the Moscow crowd on the other. To her close friends, she admitted she had little to do in Moscow and felt isolated from Israeli politics. Despite being a socialist born in Ukraine, her Jewish identity caused friction with the Soviets, making progress difficult, and by the end of her term, she felt she had accomplished little and expressed guilt for not doing more for Russian Jews, as she would have been in their position if her father had not moved to the United States. She planned to run for the first Knesset elections on 25 January 1949, returned to Israel the month before, campaigned for Mapai, which won 35% of the votes and formed a coalition, and Ben-Gurion invited her into the cabinet. She was sworn in on 8 March and served in the Knesset until 1974. Ben-Gurion initially offered her the position of deputy prime minister, which she rejected due to its vague responsibilities and the need to coordinate with many departments. Instead, she took the role of Labor Minister from 10 March 1949 to 19 June 1956, which she called her "seven beautiful years," enjoying the ability to act quickly and independently and being one of the most powerful Israeli politicians at the time. A major source of friction was funding, especially for the millions of immigrants arriving in the new state. In October 1950, Meir announced a three-year development plan with a $15 billion price tag over 15 years, securing 40% of the budget through U.S. government and American Jewish loans, while Israel Bonds contributed only a small amount, though later became a major economic contributor. Meir assisted in building over a hundred ma'abarot—temporary immigrant camps with tin-roofed huts and tents—drawing criticism from new immigrants and politicians, but defended her actions by citing limited budgets and the time needed to build permanent housing. By 1953, she helped eliminate ma'abarot, with two-thirds eliminated by 1956 and 120,000 families moved to permanent housing. Meir considered herself highly productive, implementing welfare state policies, integrating immigrants into the workforce, and launching major housing and road construction projects. From 1949 to 1956, 200,000 apartments and 30,000 houses were built, large industrial and agricultural developments began, and new hospitals, schools, and roads were constructed. Despite Finance Ministry complaints, she established social security, maternity benefits, work-related accident insurance, benefits for widows and orphans, and burial costs. In 1954, she supported Ben-Gurion against Pinhas Lavon in the Lavon Affair. In the summer of 1955, she reluctantly ran for mayor of Tel Aviv at the request of her party, lost by two votes due to the religious bloc withholding support on grounds of her gender, and was happy to rejoin the cabinet. On 3 August 1955, she was hospitalized and diagnosed with arrhythmia. In October 1955, Ben-Gurion appointed her foreign minister, replacing Sharett, due to escalating disagreements between Ben-Gurion and Sharett, and although Meir was less experienced in foreign affairs than Sharett, she had a loyal and friendly relationship with Ben-Gurion, though she disliked the lingering pro-Sharett colleagues in her department. She served as foreign minister from 18 June 1956 to 12 January 1966. Her first months as foreign minister coincided with the 1956 Suez Crisis, in which Israel, Britain, and France invaded Egypt to regain Western control of the Suez Canal, remove President Gamal Abdel Nasser, and secure freedom of navigation through the Straits of Tiran. Meir planned and coordinated with the French government and military prior to the invasion and took charge of the Israeli delegation during United Nations debates. After the fighting began, the United States, the Soviet Union, and the United Nations forced the invaders to withdraw. As foreign minister, she promoted ties with newly established African states to gain international allies, believing Israel’s experience in nation-building could serve as a model for African nations, stating that both had overcome foreign rule and faced similar challenges in reclaiming land, increasing crop yields, irrigating, raising poultry, living together, and defending themselves. She also worked to convince the United States to sell Israel weapons, achieving success in 1962 when the White House quietly agreed to sell Hawk missiles. Israel’s relationship with the Soviet Union remained frosty during her tenure. On 29 October 1957, Meir’s foot was slightly injured when a Mills bomb was thrown into the Knesset debating chamber; David Ben-Gurion and Moshe Carmel were more seriously injured. The attack was carried out by 25-year-old Moshe Dwek, born in Aleppo, whose motives were attributed to a dispute with the Jewish Agency, and he was described as mentally unbalanced. In 1958, shortly after the death of Pope Pius XII, Meir praised him for assisting the Jewish people, a legacy that remains controversial. That same year, during the wave of Jewish migration from Poland to Israel, Meir sought to prevent disabled and sick Polish Jews from immigrating, writing in a letter to Israel’s ambassador in Warsaw, Katriel Katz: "A proposal was raised in the coordination committee to inform the Polish government that we want to institute selection in aliyah, because we cannot continue accepting sick and handicapped people. Please give your opinion as to whether this can be explained to the Poles without hurting immigration." In late 1965, 67-year-old Meir was diagnosed with lymphoma. In January 1966, she retired from her role as foreign minister, citing exhaustion and ill health, though she continued to serve in the Knesset and as secretary-general of Mapai. During the 1960s, Meir lived in a flat on the upper level of a house once known as Villa Harun al-Rashid, built in 1926 by Hanna Bisharat and later rented to British officers, then given to Zionist militias due to its prominent view. According to Hanna Bisharat’s grandson George Bisharat, Meir had the front tiles sandblasted to obliterate the name "Villa Harun al-Rashid" and conceal that she was living in an Arab home. Prime Minister Levi Eshkol died suddenly on 26 February 1969, leading to the appointment of Yigal Allon as interim prime minister and an election to replace him. Before the vote, most suspected Meir would be elected. On 7 March 1969, the party’s central committee voted Meir as the new party leader. At age 71, she had mixed feelings about her health but eventually agreed, saying she would honor the party’s decision as she had all past decisions. Meir served as prime minister from 17 March 1969 to 3 June 1974, maintaining the national unity government formed after the Six-Day War, in which Mapai merged with Rafi and Ahdut HaAvoda to form the Israeli Labor Party. Six months after taking office, she led the reconfigured Alignment, comprising Labor and Mapam, into the 1969 general election, which achieved the best showing for a single party or faction in Israeli history, winning 56 seats—the only time a party approached an outright majority—and retained the national unity government. In 1969 and the early 1970s, Meir met with world leaders to promote her peace settlement ideas, including Richard Nixon (1969), Nicolae Ceaușescu (1972), and Pope Paul VI (1973), and hosted West German Chancellor Willy Brandt in Israel. In August 1970, she accepted a U.S. peace initiative calling for an end to the War of Attrition and an Israeli pledge to withdraw to "secure and recognized boundaries" in a comprehensive peace settlement. The Gahal party quit the coalition in protest, but Meir continued to lead. On 28 February 1973, during a visit to Washington, D.C., Meir agreed with Henry Kissinger’s peace proposal based on "security versus sovereignty": Israel would accept Egyptian sovereignty over all Sinai, while Egypt would accept Israeli presence in some strategic positions in Sinai. In June 1969, on the second anniversary of the Six-Day War, Meir stated in an interview with The Sunday Times on June 15, 1969, that "there was no such thing as Palestinians," a comment later described by Al Jazeera as "one of her defining – and most damning – legacies" and considered a key example of Israeli denial of Palestinian identity. In the wake of the 1972 Munich massacre, Meir appealed to the world to "save our citizens and condemn the unspeakable criminal acts committed" and ordered the Mossad to hunt down and assassinate suspected leaders and operatives of Black September and the PFLP. During the 1970s, about 200,000 Soviet Jewish emigrants were allowed to leave the Soviet Union for Israel via Austria. When seven were taken hostage at the Austria–Czechoslovakia border in September 1973 by Palestinian militants, Austrian Chancellor Bruno Kreisky closed the Jewish Agency’s transit facility in Schönau. A few days later in Vienna, Meir tried to convince Kreisky to reopen it by appealing to his Jewish heritage, calling his position "succumbing to terrorist blackmail," but Kreisky refused, so Meir returned to Israel, infuriated. A few months later, Austria opened a new transition camp. A common criticism is that she could have avoided the Yom Kippur War in 1973. For months before the attack, Egyptian President Anwar Sadat made repeated peace overtures in exchange for a full Israeli withdrawal from the Sinai, which were rebuffed by Meir, who had previously offered to discuss ceding "most of the Sinai" but refused to restore pre-1967 borders, and Egypt had no interest in peace talks under her conditions. In the days leading up to the war, Israeli intelligence could not confirm an imminent attack. On 5 October 1973, Meir received information that Syrian forces were massing on the Golan Heights and was alarmed, believing the situation resembled that before the Six-Day War. However, her advisers advised her not to worry, saying they would have adequate warning before war broke out, a view common after the Six-Day War. Despite the Knesset passing a resolution granting her power to demand a full-scale military call-up, Meir did not mobilize early. Soon, the threat became clear. Six hours before hostilities began, Meir met with Defense Minister Moshe Dayan and General David Elazar. While Dayan argued that war was unlikely and favored calling up only the air force and two divisions, Elazar advocated full-scale mobilization and a preemptive strike. On 6 October, Meir approved full-scale mobilization but rejected a preemptive strike, citing concerns that Israel might be seen as initiating hostilities, which would damage access to crucial foreign aid and military support, especially from the United States. She prioritized informing Washington of her decision. U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger later confirmed that if Israel had launched a preemptive strike, it would not have received U.S. backing. After the Yom Kippur War, Meir’s government faced infighting and questions over Israel’s lack of preparation. The Agranat Commission cleared her of "direct responsibility," stating that she wisely and quickly approved full mobilization of the reserves as recommended by the chief-of-staff, despite political considerations, performing a vital service for national defense. Her party won the December 1973 elections, but the coalition lost seats and could not form a majority. Meir resigned as prime minister on 11 April 1974 and gave up her Knesset seat on 7 June 1974, believing it was the "will of the people" and that she had served enough, stating that "five years are sufficient... It is beyond my strength to continue carrying this burden." Yitzhak Rabin succeeded her on 3 June 1974. In 1975, Meir published her autobiography, My Life, which became a New York Times Best Seller. On 21 November 1977, she spoke at the Knesset on behalf of the Labor Party to Egyptian President Anwar Sadat during his historic visit as the first Arab leader to visit Israeli-controlled territory, praising his courage and vision and expressing hope that mutual understanding could resolve differences for future generations. In May 1978, Meir was interviewed live by video link by Barbra Streisand at the finale of the American television special The Stars Salute Israel at 30, broadcast to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the state of Israel. On 8 December 1978, Meir died of lymphoma (lymphatic cancer) in Jerusalem at the age of 80 and was buried on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem. Her husband Morris Meyerson (also "Myerson") was born on 17 December 1893 in Chicago, Illinois. They married on 24 December 1917 and remained married until his death in Jerusalem on 25 May 1951. She never remarried. Despite never divorcing, the couple grew apart over time. When Meir took her children to the United States in the 1930s, Morris stayed behind in Jerusalem. Meir had two children.

Many differences remained to be resolved, that vision would be achieved in a spirit of mutual understanding.[76][77] In May 1978, Meir was interviewed live by video link by Barbra Streisand at the finale of the American television special The Stars Salute Israel at 30, broadcast to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the state of Israel.[78] On 8 December 1978, Meir died of lymphatic cancer (lymphoma) in Jerusalem at the age of 80. She was buried on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem.[79][80] Meir's husband Morris Meyerson (also "Myerson") was born on 17 December 1893 in Chicago, Illinois. They married on December 24, 1917, and remained married until his death in Jerusalem on 25 May 1951. She never remarried. Despite never divorcing, the couple grew apart over the course of the marriage. When Meir took her children with her to the United States in the 1930s, Morris stayed behind in Jerusalem.[citation needed] Meir had two children. Her son, Menachem, was born in Jerusalem in 1924 and died on 14 December 2014 in Tel Aviv. He was a professional cellist who studied at the Israel Conservatory and Manhattan School of Music.[81] Her daughter Sarah was born on 17 May 1926 and died on 30 January 2010 in Revivim.[82] She had two sisters, Sheyna (1889–1972) and Tzipke (1902–1981), as well as five other siblings who died in childhood.[citation needed] Morris, Sheyna Korngold and her husband Shamai were buried on Nahalat Yitzhak Cemetery in Givatayim.[citation needed] In 1956, after becoming Foreign Minister, she changed her surname from "Meyerson" to "Meir", meaning "illuminate", as her predecessor Moshe Sharett had all members of the foreign service take a Hebrew surname.[citation needed] She was a heavy smoker and coffee drinker, and did not exercise often, which may have contributed to her recurring heart problems.[25] Of her Jewish identity, Meir said in the 1975 edition of her autobiography My Life that: "It is not only a matter, I believe, of religious observance and practice. To me, being Jewish means and has always meant being proud to be part of a people that has maintained its distinct identity for more than 2,000 years, with all the pain and torment that has been inflicted upon it."[83] She strongly identified with Judaism culturally, but was an atheist in religious belief.[84][85][86] She is famously reported to have stated: "I believe in the Jewish people, and the Jewish people believe in God."[87] In her later years she widened her religious attitude, especially concerning the State of Israel: "This country exists as the fulfillment of a promise made by God himself. It would be ridiculous to ask it to account for its legitimacy."[88] In 1974 Meir was awarded the James Madison Award for Distinguished Public Service by Princeton University's American Whig–Cliosophic Society.[89] Also in 1974, Meir was awarded the honor of World Mother by American Mothers.[90] In 1975, Meir was awarded the Israel Prize for her special contribution to society and the State of Israel.[72][91] In 1985, Meir was inducted into the Colorado Women's Hall of Fame.[92] In 2019, Time created 89 new covers to celebrate women of the year starting from 1920; it chose her for 1956.[93] Biographer Meron Medzini argues that a perspective of forty years makes possible an appreciation of her deep nationalism and Zionism. Historians find her main legacy includes effective leadership of the Labor Movement, and building good relationships with Third World nations. Medzini states, "Apart from laying the foundations for Israel’s presence in Africa, she was never taken with the routine and often dull diplomatic work in the Foreign Ministry and abhorred its outer manifestations of ceremonies and rites."[94] Most historians agree she was a success as Secretary of Labor and Housing, but a failure as prime minister.[7] A controversial figure in Israel, she has been lionized as a founder of the state and described as the "Iron Lady" of Israeli politics, but also widely blamed for the country being caught by surprise during the 1973 Yom Kippur War. She was also criticized for her dismissive statements towards the Palestinians.[68] Meir's story has been the subject of many fictionalized portrayals. In 1977, Anne Bancroft played Meir in William Gibson's Broadway play Golda. The Australian actress Judy Davis played a young Meir in the television film A Woman Called Golda (1982), opposite Leonard Nimoy. Ingrid Bergman played the older Meir in the same film. Actress Colleen Dewhurst portrayed Meir in the 1986 TV movie Sword of Gideon.[95] In 2003, American Jewish actress Tovah Feldshuh portrayed her on Broadway in Golda's Balcony, Gibson's second play about Meir's life. The play was controversial for implying that Meir considered using nuclear weapons during the Yom Kippur War.[citation needed] Valerie Harper portrayed Meir in the touring company production and in the film version of Golda's Balcony.[96] In 2005, actress Lynn Cohen portrayed Meir in Steven Spielberg's film Munich.[citation needed] Tovah Feldshuh assumed the role of Meir again in the 2006 English-language French movie O Jerusalem. She was played by the Polish actress Beata Fudalej in the 2009 dramatic film The Hope directed by Márta Mészáros.[97] English actor Helen Mirren portrayed Meir in the 2023 biopic film Golda, directed by Guy Nattiv and produced by Michael Kuhn. The film centres on the Yom Kippur War.[98] As of April 2021, a TV miniseries Lioness starring Shira Haas is also currently being produced and will be directed by Barbra Streisand.[99] In Israel, the term "Golda's shoes" (na'alei Golda) has become a reference to the sturdy orthopedic shoes that Golda favored. These shoes were also supplied to women soldiers in the Israel Defense Forces from its foundation to 1987.[108]
